summary:
We developed a mission-oriented Earth analog assessment platform featuring two distinct similarity algorithms tailored to the different environments of the Moon and Mars, identifying suitable terrestrial sites for planetary research and equipment testing.

To address the challenge, we designed separate evaluation methods based on mission-specific environmental features. For the Moon, we compared illumination, extreme temperatures, terrain, and cold-trap conditions using a weighted arithmetic mean. For Mars, we evaluated landing surfaces, subsurface ice, hydrated minerals, ice-related terrain, and dust and weather conditions using an equally weighted geometric mean. Both algorithms integrate NASA and other scientific datasets to quantify environmental similarity.

To assess reliability, we compared our rankings with established planetary analog sites, including Mauna Kea, the Antarctic Dry Valleys, and Devon Island/Haughton Crater, which ranked among our top candidates. Replacing NASA POWER temperature data with MODIS yielded ranking correlations of 0.92–0.94, indicating strong consistency.

Since no Earth location can fully replicate lunar or Martian conditions, our tailored algorithms enable mission-specific comparisons, helping researchers identify suitable testing environments, understand their limitations, and support future planetary exploration planning.
details:
Earth Analog Finder: Mission-Driven Earth Analogs for the Moon and Mars

Before astronauts and rovers go to the Moon or Mars, they rehearse on Earth. Analog sites, however, are often chosen by how they look or by tradition. Earth Analog Finder ranks Earth locations by how well they meet specific mission test requirements, using NASA and other open data. In doing so, it finds new candidate sites and confirms known ones.

Key Findings

  • New analog candidates: Northern Yakutia, Russia scores 76.6 / 100 for the lunar long darkness & extreme cold mission, ahead of the classic Devon Island/Haughton analog (74.4). For cold-trap resources, the Lake Hazen area of northern Ellesmere Island ranks first (59.3). For terrain & mobility, Chile’s Elqui Valley Andes match the steep Malapert Massif at 90.2, and the Southern Highlands of Papua New Guinea match the Shackleton connecting ridge at 89.8. None of these sites is on our list of established analogs.
  • Validated against known analogs: Our ranking was not given any prior list of analog sites, yet it places Mauna Kea (up to 93.4 for terrain), the Antarctic Dry Valleys (88.9), and Devon Island/Haughton Crater (74.4 for darkness & cold) among the top candidates.
  • Robust to data source: Replacing NASA POWER temperature data with MODIS gives Spearman rank correlations of 0.92–0.94.
  • Efficient test planning: 5 Earth sites cover all 27 Mars target–mission tests (7 Mars targets), each at ≥ 90% of that test’s best score; a single site already covers 15 of them.
  • Looks alike ≠ tests alike: Death Valley, often shown as a Moon-like landscape, scores only 7.1 / 100 for long darkness & extreme cold and 24.5 for low-sun illumination once mission requirements are applied.

What It Does

Moon: four mission types (low-sun-angle illumination & solar power, extreme thermal environments, terrain & mobility, cold-trap resources) across ten lunar targets. The platform first checks whether a lunar target suits the mission, then lists the three most and three least similar Earth sites. Each site comes with coordinates, terrain, a suitability explanation, imagery, and a label marking it as an established or a new analog.

Mars: a three-step workflow: Select a Mission → Select a Mars Target → Explore Earth Analogs. It covers seven regions: Jezero, Gale, Arcadia, Oxia, Meridiani, Protonilus, and AP-105. Results include the most and least similar sites, five-dimension environmental profiles, global similarity grids, and a minimum test-site planner.

How It Works

  • Mars: We use features chosen for each mission: landing surface, shallow subsurface ice, hydrated minerals, ice-related terrain, dust, and near-surface meteorology. Each similarity score is an equally weighted geometric mean of these features, so a poor match on any critical feature pulls the whole score down. The data come from NASA MODIS, MERRA-2, ASTER, USGS, SWIM, and the Mars Climate Database.
  • Moon: Lunar datasets are less complete, so we use a weighted arithmetic mean with data-applicability coefficients. Terrain missions compare slope distributions and local relief with the lunar target, using NASA LRO LOLA topography. Other missions score Earth sites against the most extreme conditions Earth can actually reach, for example −89 °C as the minimum temperature and 120 h of continuous darkness. Inputs are illumination geometry, topography, MODIS land surface temperature, and peer-reviewed literature.
  • Transparency: Every score links to its feature values, formula, and data sources.

Why It’s Creative

  • From similarity to suitability: We ask “can this mission be tested here?”, not only “does it look like the Moon?”
  • Planet-specific frameworks: The Moon and Mars use different scoring methods, matched to their different data and research goals.
  • Positive and negative comparisons: Showing the least similar sites makes the reasons behind each recommendation clear.
  • Data gaps as findings: Missions without reliable data stay unscored on purpose. For example, visual navigation has no score because global image-texture data is lacking.
  • Planning, not just ranking: The minimum test-site planner reduces how many field sites a team needs.

Impact

  • Helps mission planners screen Earth sites for testing equipment, mobility systems, resource prospecting, and environmental adaptation.
  • Cuts the cost of field campaigns by finding site combinations that cover several tests.
  • Gives students and the public a bilingual (English / 繁體中文), map-based way to explore NASA open data.

Tools

Frontend: Vue, TypeScript, Leaflet · Backend: Python, FastAPI · Deployment: Docker, Nginx
Data: NASA LRO LOLA & LROC, MODIS, MERRA-2, ASTER, POWER; USGS; SWIM; Mars Climate Database; peer-reviewed literature

Limitations

  • Gravity, atmospheric pressure, and radiation cannot be reproduced on Earth.
  • Datasets differ in resolution, time period, and measurement method.
  • Scores depend on which features, weights, and reference conditions are chosen. Lunar and Martian scores use different frameworks and should not be compared directly.
  • Lunar imagery may cover only part of a target region, and we label image coverage on the site.
  • This is a preliminary screening tool. It does not certify landing safety, base feasibility, or mission success.
